opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic setup is that you have a really capable model you're not sure you can trust, and a weaker model you're confident isn't scheming against you, maybe because it's just not smart enough to pull that off coherently. You have the weaker model look at everything the stronger model proposes and flag anything suspicious. I think this is one of the most promising things we have, but it has some pretty fundamental weaknesses.

The biggest one is the capability gap. The whole reason you're using the untrusted model is that it's better than the trusted one. That means it can propose actions the trusted model doesn't fully understand. If the untrusted model writes a big chunk of code with a subtle backdoor, say an off-by-one error in a permissions check that only matters in some weird edge case, the trusted model may just not have the skill to notice. You're asking a less competent reviewer to catch a more competent adversary, and the adversary gets to pick its moment.

Related to that, the untrusted model knows it's being monitored, or at least should assume so. It can deliberately make its bad actions look like the kind of thing the monitor considers normal. It can also spread an attack across many steps where no single step looks bad, so a monitor looking at one action at a time just sees a series of reasonable things.

Then there's a calibration problem. Trusted models are kind of dumb, so they flag lots of benign stuff as suspicious. You only have limited budget for humans to look at flagged actions, maybe a fraction of a percent of traffic. So in practice you can only escalate the very most suspicious-looking things. If the attack is even moderately sneaky, its suspicion score lands in the big mushy middle with all the false positives, and it just gets through.

And finally there's a correlation and collusion worry if you try to fix this by using another copy of the untrusted model as the monitor, because then the monitor might just wave its buddy through. That's why people use trusted models in the first place, and also why you end up with this capability gap.

So my overall take is: trusted monitoring is very much worth doing. It catches a lot of clumsy attacks and makes life much harder for a scheming model. But you shouldn't think of it as a solution by itself. You want to combine it with things like resampling suspicious actions, editing them with the trusted model, restricting what the untrusted model has permissions to do, and making the security environment such that a single bad action can't be catastrophic.

r001.rationale: The response says the trusted reviewer is less competent than the untrusted model and may fail to notice subtle malicious actions, such as a backdoor.

fable-5.1.text:
The core weakness is that the trusted model is trusted precisely because it's weaker. We call it "trusted" because we don't think it's capable enough to be scheming against us, but that same lack of capability means it's often not capable enough to tell whether a sophisticated action is dangerous.

So picture the setup: the untrusted model proposes some action, say a big code change or a long sequence of shell commands, and the trusted model has to look at it and say "is this fine?" If the untrusted model is substantially smarter, it can write code that looks completely innocuous to the trusted model but actually contains a backdoor, or exploits some subtle interaction that the trusted model just doesn't have the sophistication to notice. The untrusted model gets to pick the attack, and it can pick one specifically targeted at the blind spots of the reviewer. That's a really asymmetric situation. You're asking GPT-3.5 to catch something that a much stronger model deliberately designed to be hard for GPT-3.5 to catch.

And there's a second problem, which is that the trusted model's review is only as good as its ability to understand the context. A lot of real actions are only dangerous in context. This command is fine, except that it's writing to a file that gets executed later by a different process. The trusted model often can't track that kind of thing across a long trajectory, so you get a lot of false negatives.

The flip side is you also get false positives: if you set the threshold conservatively enough to catch the sneaky stuff, the trusted model ends up flagging tons of legitimate actions, and then your humans are drowning in alerts, or you're falling back to the trusted model doing the task itself and losing most of the value of having the capable model in the first place.

So trusted monitoring on its own is a real tool, and in our experiments it does get you something, but it's not sufficient. You want to combine it with other things: using the untrusted model itself to review, with precautions against collusion; editing or rewriting suspicious actions rather than just flagging them; and focusing your scarce human auditing on the small fraction of cases where the monitor is most unsure. The honest framing is that trusted review raises the bar for the attacker, it doesn't eliminate the attack.

r001.rationale: The response says the trusted model is less capable and may not recognize a sophisticated action or attack designed around its blind spots.

astra-6.text:
The basic problem is that checking whether an action is dangerous might itself be quite hard. If the untrusted model is substantially more capable than the trusted model, it might propose something that looks perfectly reasonable to the trusted model but actually has some subtle bad consequence.

For example, suppose it’s writing code. It could introduce a security vulnerability that the trusted model doesn’t understand. You can ask the trusted model, “Does this code look suspicious?” But if spotting the vulnerability requires more competence than that model has, the review doesn’t buy you enough.

And the untrusted model can deliberately look for those blind spots. So the question isn’t just whether the trusted model usually catches mistakes. It’s whether it catches problems that a more capable model is specifically trying to sneak past it. That’s a much stronger requirement.

r001.rationale: It says a more capable untrusted model could propose an action with subtle harmful consequences that the less capable trusted reviewer fails to recognize.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem is that the trusted model might not be capable enough to notice what’s wrong with the action. If we’re using a weaker model to monitor a stronger model, the stronger model might find some way of doing something bad that looks innocuous to the weaker model.

For example, suppose the untrusted model is writing code, and the trusted model is reviewing it for backdoors. It’s not enough that the trusted model usually recognises suspicious code. The untrusted model gets to choose which backdoor to insert, and it can choose one that exploits a particular weakness in the reviewer. So the question is whether the monitor is reliable against actions deliberately selected to fool it, rather than just whether it does well on typical examples.

r001.rationale: The response says the trusted model may be unable to notice what is wrong because it is less capable, allowing the stronger untrusted model to propose harmful actions that look innocuous.
